questionStem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 38 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in labor. She had spontaneous rupture of membranes 32 hours ago. At 35 weeks' gestation , results of a rectovaginal culture for group B streptococcal infection were positive . Her temperature is 38.8°C (101 .8°F). The lungs are clear to auscultation . The uterus is tender to palpation . There is no costovertebral angle tenderness . A fetal heart tracing is shown. The cervix is 80% effaced and 3 cm dilated ; the vertex is at -1 station . Her leukocyte count is 19,200/mm 3 with a left shift. Microscopic examination of a catheterized urine specimen shows no WBCs or bacteria . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this fetal heart tracing pattern?

choices.D: True knot in the umbilical cord

correctExplanation: Fetal tachycardia is defined as a heart rate greater than 160/min. Fetal tachycardia can be caused by hypoxia, fetal anemia, intrauterine infection, and maternal medications. Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in the setting of premature or prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 hours prior to delivery). Risk factors for prolonged rupture of membranes include young maternal age, smoking, low socioeconomic status, and a history of sexually transmitted infections. Chorioamnionitis typically presents with fever and abdominal pain, along with uterine tenderness to palpation on physical examination. The amniotic fluid may be foul smelling. Leukocytosis on laboratory evaluation is also typically present. Complications include infection of the fetus with pneumonia or bacteremia. Treatment involves the administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, most commonly ampicillin and gentamicin, and the induction of labor. Following delivery, the neonate will need close monitoring for infection, with a majority requiring antibiotic therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oligohydramnios (Choice B) presents with a low amniotic fluid index, and can result from premature rupture of membranes, postdate pregnancies, or abnormalities of the fetal genitourinary tract. Complications include intrauterine growth restriction; umbilical cord compression, which would present with variable decelerations on fetal heart rate tracing; pulmonary hypoplasia; and perinatal mortality. Pyelonephritis (Choice C) classically presents with lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency), flank pain, fever, and leukocytosis with evidence of urinary tract infection on urinalysis with pyuria, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, and bacteria. This patient's urinalysis is negative for infection, making pyelonephritis unlikely. True knot in the umbilical cord (Choice D) would lead to fetal hypoxemia with resultant changes in the fetal heart rate. However, these are relatively rare and fetal distress secondary to an umbilical knot more commonly occurs with descent through the vaginal canal, as the transition puts the most stress on the umbilical cord. It is less likely a cause of this patient's presentation than an intrauterine infection. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) can cause late decelerations and is most commonly caused by hypertension, cocaine use, placental abruption, anemia, diabetes, and cigarette smoking. It would not explain this patient's findings of uterine pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Educational Objective: Chorioamnionitis is a polymicrobial bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in the setting of premature or prolonged rupture of membranes. It typically presents with fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis. It can lead to fetal tachycardia on fetal monitoring, and following delivery, the neonate will need close monitoring for infection, with a majority requiring antibiotic therapy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A hospitalized 42-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 40 weeks' gestation has a cervix that has remained 6 cm dilated and completely effaced for 3 hours. The fetus has an estimated weight of 3487 g (7 lb 11 oz) and is in the left occiput posterior position . Contractions occur every 5 minutes , last 30 seconds , and are 30 mm Hg in pressure . Her first pregnancy ended in spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3629-g (8-lb) boy 3 years ago. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the arrest of labor?
correctExplanation: Labor consists of three defined stages. The first stage encompasses the start of labor (contractions and cervical change) until the completion of cervical dilation and effacement. The second stage includes the time from complete cervical dilation to the baby's birth, and the third stage contains the delivery of the placenta. The first stage of labor is divided into a latent stage and active stage, based on the degree of cervical dilation, with the active stage beginning after 4 cm of cervical dilation is achieved. The active stage of labor can be protracted, which occurs when the cervix is dilating at less than 1 to 2 cm/hour, as seen in this patient, or arrested, in which case there is no cervical change for greater than 4 hours with adequate contractions or no cervical change for greater than 6 hours with inadequate contractions. Abnormal progression of the active stage of labor can be caused by hypotonic contractions, cephalopelvic distortion, and a non-occiput anterior fetal presentation. Inadequate contractions are defined as occurring less than three or four times in a 10-minute period with a strength less than 200 Montevideo units. Montevideo units are calculated by summing the strength of each uterine contraction (uterine peak pressure minus baseline pressure) over a 10- minute interval. This patient demonstrates contractions every 5 minutes that are 30 mm Hg in pressure (60 Montevideo units). This indicates that the inadequate, hypotonic contractions are the most likely cause of this patient's protraction of active labor. Protraction of the active phase of labor can be managed with oxytocin to augment uterine contractions and prostaglandins to assist in cervical ripening, whereas arrest of the active phase of labor is managed with cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cephalopelvic disproportion (Choice A) can cause protraction or arrest of labor. It more commonly presents with molding of the fetal head and caput succedaneum. It is less likely in this patient, as she previously had a successful vaginal delivery of a larger fetus. Fetal macrosomia (Choice B) is defined as a fetal weight above 4000 g and can cause protraction or arrest of labor as a result of the inability of the fetus to pass through the pelvic inlet. However, this patient's fetus is only 3487 g, making this an unlikely cause of her protracted labor. Advanced maternal age (Choice D) increases the risk for chromosomal abnormalities, spontaneous abortion, placenta previa, abruptio placenta, and preterm delivery. However, it is not a risk factor for protracted labor. Occiput posterior position (Choice E) can cause protraction or arrest of labor but more commonly presents with molding of the fetal head and caput succedaneum. While present in this patient, it is less likely responsible for the protraction of labor than her weak uterine contractions. Educational Objective: Inadequate uterine contractions can lead to protraction or arrest of the active phase of labor. Adequate contractions occur three to four times in 10 minutes with a strength of 200 Montevideo units. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 33 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because she has had fluid leaking from her vagina for 2 days. Her fetus is active , and she has not had any uterine contractions . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 32-week gestation. The fetal heart rate is 140/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: Sterile speculum examination of the vagina

correctExplanation: Premature rupture of membranes is the rupture of the amniotic sac before the onset of labor (regular contractions plus cervical change). If it occurs before 37 weeks' gestation, it is termed preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). Patients typically report a gush of fluid or steady leakage of fluid from the vagina. Initial evaluation includes a sterile speculum examination of the vagina, which may show pooling of amniotic fluid or leakage of fluid from the cervical os. Nitrazine testing of the fluid will disclose a pH of 7.0 to 7.3, and terning will be seen on microscopic examination. Ultrasonography can also be utilized to determine the amount of residual amniotic fluid, which would be decreased in the setting of the rupture of membranes. Risk factors include previous premature rupture of membranes, a vaginal or cervical infection, and cigarette smoking. Treatment involves expectant management, with betamethasone administered to accelerate fetal lung maturity in patients with a gestational age less than 34 weeks. Screening for sexually transmitted infections and Streptococcus aga/actiae (group B) should also be completed. Antibiotics are commonly administered prophylactically because of an increased risk for chorioamnionitis. Other complications include preterm birth, cord compression, abruptio placentae, and postpartum endometritis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fetal fibronectin test (Choice A) is used to determine whether a patient is in true or false labor and can determine the likelihood of delivery within 7 to 10 days of testing when present in the cervicovaginal fluid. It does not play a role in the determination of preterm premature rupture of membranes. Fetal scalp electrode monitoring (Choice B) is used to determine fetal cardiac activity and heart rate. It is most used when external (eg, Doppler) monitoring is ineffective in determining fetal heart rate. However, it can only be done after membranes have ruptured, so the initial first step is determining whether this patient's membranes are intact. Digital examination of the cervix (Choice C) is completed to determine dilation and effacement of the cervix, which is important in determining the progression of labor. However, this should not be completed until a sterile speculum examination has been performed. Amniocentesis (Choice E) is an invasive sampling of amniotic fluid through the abdominal wall, usually performed at 15 to 20 weeks, to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities. It can also be used in the evaluation of chorioamnionitis but is not useful in the evaluation of premature rupture of membranes. Educational Objective: Preterm premature rupture of membranes is the rupture of the amniotic sac before the onset of labor in pregnancies less than 37 weeks' gestation. Initial evaluation includes a sterile speculum examination to assess for pooling of fluid in the vagina, followed by a phenaphthazine test and microscopic examination of the vaginal fluid to assess for terning. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 87-year-old woman who is a nursing home resident is brought to the physician 1 week after the staff noticed a vaginal mass. She has dementia, Alzheimer type , and appears disoriented . Examination shows partial prolapse of the uterine cervix through the introitus . The uterus can be easily pushed back into the pelvis. There is no cervical ulceration . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Normal pelvic support is caused by the action of several pelvic muscles and ligaments, including the levator muscles, urogenital diaphragm, perinea! body, endopelvic fascia, uterosacral and cardinal ligaments, anal sphincter, and urethral sphincter. Defects in this pelvic support may result in urogenital prolapse, which is because of the loss of connective tissue and muscular support of the uterus, paravaginal tissue, bladder wall, urethra, or distal rectum. Risk factors for pelvic support defects include collagen and other connective tissue disorders, vaginal delivery, menopause, prior pelvic surgery, and increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, obesity and chronic constipation). Signs and symptoms include a vaginal mass, vaginal pressure, perinea! discomfort, and urinary or fecal retention or incontinence. Management may include the insertion of a vaginal pessary, which is a mechanical device that provides pelvic support, along with pelvic floor exercises. If noninvasive therapies fail, surgical treatment with reconstruction, fixation, uterine suspension, or hysterectomy can be considered.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Pelvic ultrasonography (Choice A) has no role in diagnosing pelvic support defects. Evaluation of pelvic support defects is clinical with a speculum examination, and may also include urinalysis, cystoscopy, or evaluation of post-void residual volume. Endometrial biopsy (Choice B) is used in the evaluation for abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in women over 45 years of age or in postmenopausal women for the investigation of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Cervical amputation (Choice D) and vaginal hysterectomy (Choice E) may be used in the treatment of pelvic support defects, however, surgical management of uterine prolapse is typically considered later, after attempting noninvasive management. These techniques may be difficult to ethically justify in an elderly person with dementia depending on the patient's goals of care and relative safety for surgery. Educational Objective: Pelvic support defects causing urogenital prolapse are typically to the result of the loss of connective tissue and muscular support of the uterus, paravaginal tissue, bladder wall, urethra, or distal rectum. Management may include the insertion of a vaginal pessary, which is a mechanical device that improves pelvic support, along with pelvic floor exercises. If noninvasive therapies fail, surgical treatment with reconstruction, fixation, uterine suspension, or hysterectomy can be considered. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 27-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 1, aborta 1, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She reports that she has felt little movement of the fetus during the past 18 hours. Pregnancy had been uncomplicated . She weighed 59 kg (130 lb) prior to her pregnancy ; BMI was 22 kg/m 2• She has had a 9.5-kg (28-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy . Her pulse is 72/min , and blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. The fundal height is 29 cm. No fetal heart tones are heard on Doppler. On pelvic examination , the cervix is closed and not effaced . Urine dipstick shows no glucose or protein. Ultrasonography confirms the absence of fetal cardiac activity in an otherwise normal-appearing male fetus . The patient and her husband choose to return home to await spontaneous labor. Four weeks later, the patient comes to the physician because of an episode of light vaginal bleeding but no contractions . External electronic monitoring shows mild irregular contractions every 20 to 30 minutes . The cervix is closed and not effaced , and the presenting part is soft and at -2 station . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Hematocrit Platelet count Plasma fibrinogen 11 g/dL 32% 90,000/mm 3 250 mg/dL (N=20-400) Stillbirth refers to fetal demise after 20 weeks' gestation and can occur before or during delivery. Antepartum intrauterine fetal demise commonly presents as in this patient, with decreased fetal movement and lack of fetal heart tones on examination. Ultrasonography confirms the intrauterine fetal demise. In high-income countries, stillbirth is most commonly because of chromosomal abnormalities, uteroplacental insufficiency, and maternal medical disease, whereas it is more commonly caused by maternal infection, preeclampsia, or obstructed labor in low-income countries. Delivery for antepartum intrauterine fetal demise is based on the mother's wishes, with immediate induction or delayed natural delivery; both options in the absence of any complicating medical issues. Labor typically begins 1 to 2 weeks after fetal demise. Coagulation abnormalities can occur with delayed delivery because of the release of tissue factor {thromboplastin) from the placenta. This can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation {DIC), which presents with thrombocytopenia, prolongation of partial thromboplastin and prothrombin time, increased d-dimer concentration, and decreased fibrinogen concentration. Given this patient's early mild contractions, closed cervix, prolonged retention of a nonviable fetus, and risk for the development of coagulation abnormalities, induction of labor is the most appropriate next step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma {Choice B) is typically performed in patients with coagulation abnormalities that put them at increased risk for bleeding, such as supratherapeutic international normalized ratio {INR) or DIC. As this patient has yet to develop coagulation abnormalities, treatment with fresh frozen plasma is inappropriate. Transfusion of platelets {Choice C) is indicated when a patient's platelets fall below 10,000/mm 3 or below 50,000/mm 3 when they are actively bleeding or require a surgical intervention or invasive procedure. This patient's platelets are 90,000/mm 3, making a platelet transfusion inappropriate at this time. Cesarean delivery {Choice D) can be used to deliver fetuses in the setting of arrest of labor, cephalopelvic disproportion, and placenta or vasa previa but is not typically required in intrauterine fetal demise. Following fetal death, there is a collapse and maceration of the fetal body, which allows most fetuses to undergo successful vaginal delivery. Dilation and curettage {Choice E) can be used in elective abortion or to remove remaining fetal tissue in a missed or incomplete spontaneous abortion. However, as this fetal demise occurred at 32 weeks, the fetus is likely too large to be removed with dilation and curettage. Educational Objective: Stillbirth refers to the demise of a fetus after 20 weeks' gestation and can occur before or during delivery. For antepartum intrauterine fetal demise, immediate induction or delayed natural labor are both options, but prolonged retention of a nonviable fetus increases the risk for developing DIC in the mother because of the release of thromboplastin from the placenta. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 25-year-old primigravid woman is in labor at 24 weeks' gestation . Treatment with a tocolytic agent is ineffective . She has used crack cocaine during the pregnancy . Cocaine most likely altered her uterine contractility by which of the following mechanisms?
correctExplanation: Crack cocaine is a sympathomimetic that increases sympathetic tone through the inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. This results in an increased synaptic norepinephrine concentration and consequent increased adrenergic receptor activation. This increased sympathetic tone results in the activation of aradrenergic receptors on the uterine myometrial smooth muscle myocytes, leading to increased contraction. This abnormally increased, unregulated contraction of uterine smooth muscle can result in the onset of preterm labor. Tocolytic therapy with common agents such as terbutaline (~-mimetic), magnesium sulfate, prostaglandin inhibitors, and calcium channel blockers are often ineffective at reducing uterine contractions, as they do not directly inhibit the sympathetic activation of the uterine myocytes, which is increased in the setting of cocaine use. Cocaine use in pregnancy can also cause uteroplacental insufficiency with low birth weight or intrauterine growth restriction, miscarriage, and abruptio placentae as a result of sympathetic stimulation and resultant vasoconstriction.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreasing catecholamines (Choice A) would cause relaxation of the uterine smooth muscle. However, cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine in the synapse, increasing sympathetic tone and uterine contractility. Decreasing parasympathetic tone (Choice B) may lead to smooth muscle contraction because of a relative increase in sympathetic tone compared to parasympathetic tone, but this is not the mechanism of action of crack cocaine. Increasing norepinephrine reuptake (Choice D) would decrease the amount of norepinephrine available for adrenergic receptor stimulation, which would cause a relative decrease in sympathetic stimulation and a decrease in smooth muscle contraction. Cocaine, on the contrary, inhibits norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. Increasing parasympathetic tone (Choice E) would lead to uterine smooth muscle relaxation, rather than contraction, as seen in this patient. This is not the mechanism of crack cocaine. Educational Objective: Crack cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic because of the inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. In pregnancy, this increased sympathetic tone increases the risk for abnormal uterine smooth muscle contractions and potential preterm labor. Cocaine is also associated with an increased risk for uteroplacental insufficiency, miscarriage, low birth weight, and abruptio placentae. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: Two days after spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy newborn at term, a previously healthy 37-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, has left-sided pleuritic chest pain and progressive shortness of breath . Her pulse is 94/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 96/55 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 89%. Breath sounds are normal bilaterally. Examination of the extremities shows mild edema and no tenderness . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9.1 g/dl , and leukocyte count is 15,500/mm 3• Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows : Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.C: Fetal squamous cells in the pulmonary veins

correctExplanation: 7.45 21 mm Hg 85 mm Hg Pulmonary embolism classically presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and clear breath sounds, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state (eg, pregnancy). Small pulmonary emboli may present only as pain or subjective shortness of breath and may be asymptomatic with normal vital signs. By contrast, large emboli with pulmonary infarctions generally cause more severe symptoms, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, and potentially hypotension if significant enough to obstruct cardiac output. The resultant tachypnea is demonstrated on arterial blood gas analysis as an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation leading to diminished arterial carbon dioxide, and as hypoxemia because of the ventilated but not perfused affected lung segments. Pelvic venous congestion is a common source of deep venous thrombosis in pregnancy. Large pulmonary emboli may be seen on chest x-ray by secondary signs, such as wedge-shaped areas of infarction or via the Westermark sign of unilateral oligemia, though the standard of diagnosis is CT pulmonary angiography. In pregnancy, a ventilation-perfusion scan may be preferred as this technique is safer for the fetus (less radiation exposure). The ECG in a pulmonary embolus often shows sinus tachycardia, and if there is right heart strain can exhibit right axis deviation, S wave in lead I, Q wave in lead 111, and inverted T wave in lead Ill ('S1Q3T3'). Treatment depends on the risk for bleeding to the patient but includes systemic anticoagulation or surgical thrombectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Bronchial smooth muscle contractions (Choice A) describe the pathophysiology of asthma and reactive airway disease. Obstruction to airflow through constricted small airways presents with shortness of breath and wheezing, hyperventilation or hypoventilation if severe, and generally with vital signs reflecting tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Examination shows wheezing and respiratory distress. This patient's breath sounds are clear, making this a less likely diagnosis. Exudates in the alveoli (Choice B) describes pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome. Pneumonia presents with cough, pleuritic chest pain, fever, and chills, and often follows an upper respiratory infection or aspiration event. Vital signs may be normal or show signs of sepsis (tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia). Auscultation generally discloses focal or diffuse rhonchi and egophony; examination may show dullness to percussion. Fetal squamous cells in the pulmonary veins (Choice C) describe an amniotic fluid embolism, a rare and life-threatening complication that occurs when amniotic fluid enters maternal circulation. It classically presents with acute, severe shortness of breath, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy during labor. It would be less likely to occur 2 days following delivery. Mucus trapping in the bronchioles (Choice D) describes the pathophysiology of acute or chronic bronchitis, or cystic fibrosis. These entities present with cough productive of sputum, and rhonchorous breath sounds. Educational Objective: Pulmonary embolism classically presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and clear breath sounds, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state (eg, pregnancy). The resultant tachypnea is demonstrated on arterial blood gas analysis as an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation and as hypoxemia because of the ventilated but not perfused affected lung segments. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman with leiomyomata uteri comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . She has not had vaginal bleeding , pelvic pain, or loss of urine. Examination shows no abnormalities except for a uterus consistent in size with a 15-week gestation . Her hematocrit is 41 %. Pelvic ultrasonography confirms leiomyomata uteri. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: In this patient with asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri (also known as uterine fibroids), the most appropriate management is observation only. Leiomyomata uteri are common benign tumors of the uterine smooth muscle. In many patients, leiomyomata uteri are asymptomatic, though in other patients, leiomyomata uteri can lead to abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain or pressure, and/or reproductive dysfunction. Physical examination may demonstrate an enlarged, lobulated uterus, and the presence of leiomyomata uteri can be confirmed with ultrasonography. Since leiomyomata uteri are benign and may regress over time or with menopause, asymptomatic lesions should be managed expectantly. For symptomatic leiomyomata uteri, hysteroscopic or abdominal myomectomy is often the first-line treatment. In patients who do not desire pregnancy, alternative treatments include oral contraceptive therapy, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist therapy, and hysterectomy (oral contraceptive and GnRH agonist therapy can lead to rebound symptoms when discontinued to allow for conception).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous pyelography (Choice B) is utilized to visualize the urinary tract, not the uterus. In intravenous pyelography, iodine contrast dye is injected, and imaging is obtained when the contrast fills the lumen of the urinary tract to disclose tract pathology, such as nephrolithiasis, tumors, and strictures. Myomectomy (Choice E) is a first-line treatment option for symptomatic uterine fibroids, which involves the surgical removal of one or multiple specific leiomyomata uteri. GnRH agonist therapy (Choice C), oral contraceptive therapy (Choice D), and hysterectomy are also treatment considerations for symptomatic leiomyomata uteri in patients who do not desire to preserve fertility. However, any of these options should only be considered for patients with symptomatic leiomyomata uteri, not for this patient without symptoms. Educational Objective: Leiomyomata uteri are common benign tumors of the smooth muscle. Asymptomatic leiomyomata uteri are managed expectantly with observation, while leiomyomata uteri that cause symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, or reproductive dysfunction can be managed with myomectomy (leiomyomata uteri removal), oral contraceptive therapy, GnRH therapy agonists, or hysterectomy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She has no history of operative procedures , and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . She has a 3-year history of hypothyroidism well controlled with levothyroxine . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall. She weighed 77 kg (169 lb) prior to her pregnancy ; BMI was 29 kg/m 2• She has had a 14-kg (31-lb) weight gain during her pregnancy . Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Fundal height is 30 cm. Ultrasonography shows moderate polyhydramnios . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings ?
correctExplanation: Polyhydramnios refers to excessive concentrations of amniotic fluid volume and an associated increased uterine size relative to gestational age. It is associated with an increased risk for fetal anomalies, placental abruption, preterm labor, and postpartum uterine atony. It should be suspected when the uterine size and fundal height are larger than expected for gestational age. Polyhydramnios can be diagnosed on ultrasonography examination through measuring the amniotic fluid index (AFI). An AFI greater than 24 cm indicates an excessive amount of amniotic fluid. Polyhydramnios can be idiopathic or associated with a variety of disorders, including maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B 19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities such as duodenal atresia or anencephaly. Fetal anomalies are the most common cause of polyhydramnios but are typically apparent on ultrasonography. Antenatal testing, such as fetal ultrasonography with biophysical profile, should be performed to evaluate for underlying fetal anomalies along with an amniocentesis to evaluate for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities. The frequency of antenatal testing depends on the severity of the polyhydramnios. Given the patient's history of an uncomplicated pregnancy until this point, the most likely cause of this patient's polyhydramnios is undiagnosed maternal diabetes mellitus.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Excessive maternal hydration {Choice A) may lead to peripheral edema and hypervolemic hyponatremia but would be unlikely to alter the amount of amniotic fluid. Fetal aneuploidy {Choice B) can present with polyhydramnios but would be expected to also have apparent congenital abnormalities on ultrasonography. For example, when combined with intrauterine growth restriction, polyhydramnios is commonly as a result oftrisomy 18, which would present with rounded feet, cystic hygroma, neural tube defects, facial defects, omphalocele, and septal or valvular cardiac disease. Fetal myotonic dystrophy {Choice C) presents with hypotonia, joint contractures, respiratory muscle weakness, and bilateral facial paralysis. Polyhydramnios is common; however, inheritance is autosomal dominant, and thus the disorder would be unlikely in this patient with no family history of myotonic dystrophy. Fetal renal agenesis {Choice D) would cause oligohydramnios because of the absence of urine production, not polyhydramnios as seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Polyhydramnios can be caused by maternal diabetes mellitus, fetal infection with parvovirus B19, twin-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities (eg, duodenal atresia, anencephaly, esophageal atresia). r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A married 37-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, at 17 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She is Rh-negative , and an antibody screening at 12 weeks' gestation was negative . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Amniocentesis is done , and the amniotic fluid is grossly bloody. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Serial measurement of fetal antibody titers
choices.B: Serial measurement of maternal antibody titers
choices.C: Maternal intramuscular administration of pooled immune globulin now
choices.D: Maternal intramuscular administration of Rho(Q) immune globulin now
choices.E: Maternal intramuscular administration of Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation and after delivery
choices.F: Maternal intravenous administration of corticosteroids now
choices.G: Fetal transfusion of Rh-negative blood now
choices.H: Fetal transfusion of Rh-positive blood now
choices.I: Amniocentesis for determination of /1 OD 450 in the late second or early third trimester

correctExplanation: F) Maternal intravenous administration of corticosteroids now G) Fetal transfusion of Rh-negative blood now H) Fetal transfusion of Rh-positive blood now I) Amniocentesis for determination of /1 OD 450 in the late second or early third trimester J) No action Rh-negative mothers are at a high risk for developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies if exposed to blood from a Rh-positive fetus. While this commonly occurs at delivery, it can also occur prior to delivery with procedures such as amniocentesis, as seen in this patient. If Rh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation enter the maternal circulation, it is possible that the mother's immune system will form antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen. This can result in severe hemolytic anemia of the fetus (erythroblastosis fetalis) as the mother's antibodies may cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of the fetus's red blood cells (RBCs). Rh0(D) immune globulin acts by binding to Rh-positive cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the immune system from developing antibodies to the Rh(D) antigen. It is commonly given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks of gestation, after delivery of an Rh-positive newborn, after any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and after any episodes of fetomaternal bleeding. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management in this patient would be to provide Rho(D) immune globulin now, in order to prevent her from developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Serial measurements of fetal antibody titers (Choice A) would not determine whether the mother has developed anti-Rh(D) antibodies in response to the amniocentesis. Frequent blood assessments of the fetus also come with associated risks, such as further bleeding, infection, and fetal death. Serial measurements of maternal antibody titers (Choice B) would allow the practitioner to determine whether she has developed anti-Rh(D) antibodies in response to the amniocentesis. However, the better option in this case would be to prevent antibody formation in the first place. Maternal intramuscular administration of pooled immune globulin now (Choice C) and maternal intravenous administration of corticosteroids (Choice F) would not provide protection against the development of anti-Rh(D) antibodies, for which this mother is at risk. Antibodies directed against Rh-positive cells would provide more adequate protection. Maternal intramuscular administration of Rh0(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks' gestation and after delivery (Choice E) would also be appropriate in this Rh-negative patient. However, without receiving Rho(D) immune globulin now, she would be at risk for developing anti-Rh(D) antibodies because of her exposure to fetal blood during the amniocentesis. Fetal transfusion of Rh-negative blood (Choice G) or Rh-positive blood (Choice H) is inappropriate, as it is not currently indicated and the fetal blood type is unknown, thus transfusion could lead to hemolytic anemia as a result of incompatible blood types. It is more appropriate to prevent the development of anti-Rh(D) antibodies and the subsequent fetal hemolytic anemia than to prophylactically treat the anemia. Amniocentesis for determination of /1 OD 450 in the late second or early third trimester (Choice I) can accurately diagnose severe fetal hemolytic anemia in the setting of Rh(D) alloimmunization, because of the presence of increased bilirubin in the amniotic fluid. However, the risk for alloimmunization can be reduced by administering Rho(D) immune globulin now. No action (Choice J) is inappropriate, as exposure to fetal blood can cause Rh(D) alloimmunization in a Rh-negative mother, which can in turn cause erythroblastosis fetalis and fetal death. It can be prevented with the administration of Rho(D) immune globulin now. Educational Objective: Rh-negative mothers are at a high risk for Rh(D) alloimmunization when exposed to Rh(D) antigens from the fetal circulation. Alloimmunization can be prevented by the administration of Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks of gestation, after delivery of an Rh(D)-positive fetus, after any invasive procedure (eg, amniocentesis), and after any episodes of fetomaternal hemorrhage. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 22-year-old primigravid woman at 27 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 5 hours after the sudden onset of increasingly severe abdominal pain and a 3-hour history of nausea , vomiting , chills , and worsening malaise . She reports good fetal movement. She has had mild uterine contractions . She has not had vaginal bleeding or loss of vaginal fluid. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness to palpation with exquisite tenderness in the right lower quadrant ; there is no guarding or rebound . On pelvic examination , the cervix is nulliparous and closed . She is unable to tolerate a bimanual examination because of extreme tenderness . Her leukocyte count is 16,700/mm 3• External fetal monitoring shows a heart rate of 170/min with moderate variability . There are spontaneous accelerations and no decelerations . An external tocometer shows intermittent uterine contractions . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Appendicitis classically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. McBurney point, a sensitive location for tenderness on palpation, is located at two-thirds the distance between the umbilicus and the inguinal ligament, because this is the common position of the appendix. In pregnancy, as a result of the location of the enlarging uterus, the appendix may be displaced superiorly as compared to that of a nongravid patient. This displacement limits the classic history and physical examination, which rely on a right lower quadrant position of the appendix. When displaced cephalad, parietal peritoneal inflammation may no longer occur at the McBurney point, even migrating as cephalad as the right upper quadrant, mimicking diagnoses such as cholecystitis. Diagnosis is facilitated by CT scans (though less ideal in pregnancy because of the risk for teratogenicity to the fetus), MRI, or ultrasonography, which may show appendiceal enlargement, the presence of an appendicolith, appendiceal wall thickening, or periappendiceal fluid or fat stranding. Fetal heart tracings are usually reassuring unless maternal hemodynamics have been compromised, and fetal tachycardia may result in response to maternal fever. Treatment is with urgent appendectomy to prevent complications such as appendiceal rupture, sepsis, preterm labor, and death.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cholecystitis (Choice B) presents with signs that may mimic some aspects of appendicitis, such as fever, nausea, abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. However, cholecystitis typically causes right upper quadrant pain that may be elicited by pressure applied to the right upper quadrant during deep inspiration and leads to termination of the breath (Murphy sign), rather than right lower quadrant pain. It is important to note that cephalad displacement of the appendix by the gravid uterus may cause appendicitis to produce right upper quadrant pain in some patients, mimicking cholecystitis. Chorioamnionitis (Choice C) is a bacterial infection of the fetal membranes and commonly occurs in the setting of premature or prolonged rupture of membranes. Maternal fever and leukocytosis are characteristic, and the uterus may be tender to palpation. Pelvic inflammatory disease (Choice D) is inflammation of the uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries, and usually occurs secondary to infection with the sexually transmitted organisms Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Peritonitis may ensue in advanced cases. The absence of abnormal cervical discharge, cervicitis, or cervical motion tenderness, as well as the presence of exquisite right lower quadrant tenderness render this a less likely diagnosis in this patient. Pyelonephritis (Choice E) typically presents with fevers, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain with associated costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination. This most commonly occurs from ascending urinary tract infections. While pregnant patients are at an increased risk for pyelonephritis, the absence of costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms render this diagnosis less likely than appendicitis. Educational Objective: Acute appendicitis may occur in gravid women and presents with right lower quadrant (or variably right-sided pain based on the location of the appendix) or periumbilical abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation. Treatment is with urgent appendectomy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 3, para 2, comes to the physician for her first prenatal visit. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago. She had a fracture of the right femur 12 months ago that required open reduction and a blood transfusion . Her current partner is the father of all her children . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with an 8-week gestation . Her blood group is 0 , Rh-negative . Indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for anti-Kell antibody at a titer of 1 :256. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: 24-Hour urine collection for measurement of protein and creatinine clearance
choices.B: Kell tyl'.)ing of the father's blood
choices.D: Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid

correctExplanation: A mother can develop antibodies against red blood cell (RBC) antigens after being exposed to fetal blood antigens during delivery or from a previous blood transfusion. In this case, this patient likely developed antibodies to the Kell RBC antigen after being exposed to it in her blood transfusion. Because maternal antibodies can cross the placenta, it is important to determine whether this patient's fetus has Kell-positive or Kell-negative RBCs. If her fetus had Kell-positive RBCs, the antibodies created by her immune system would cause hemolysis of the fetal erythrocytes, leading to severe fetal hemolytic anemia (eg, erythroblastosis fetalis) and likely fetal demise. As the mother has no signs of hemolysis in the presence of anti-Kell antibodies, her RBCs do not have Kell antigens and she would not have contributed a Kell antigen to her fetus. The easiest way to determine the antigen status of the fetus is to determine the antigen status of the father. If he is Kell-negative as well, then the fetus will be Kell-negative and there is no risk for erythroblastosis fetalis. However, if he is positive, there is a possibility that their child will be Kell antigen-positive and suffer from erythroblastosis fetalis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. 24-Hour urine collection for measurement of protein and creatinine clearance (Choice A) is used to diagnose preeclampsia in the setting of hypertension. However, this patient is at only 8 weeks of gestation, whereas preeclampsia typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. Liver function tests (Choice C) would demonstrate abnormalities in transaminases or bilirubin and may be useful in the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets). It also typically presents after 20 weeks of gestation. Measurement of bilirubin concentration in amniotic fluid (Choice D) can be used to determine whether the fetus is experiencing hemolysis. However, sampling would be unnecessary if Kell typing of the father disclosed that he was Kell-negative, making this an inappropriate initial action. Intravenous lgG therapy (Choice E) can be used to treat autoimmune diseases and could have possibly prevented the development of Kell antibodies if it had been given at the time of blood transfusion. However, it plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis in the setting of active anti-Kell antibodies. Intravenous Rh0(D) immune globulin therapy (Choice F) is used to prevent alloimmunization to the Rh(D) antigen in Rh(D)-negative women when they are potentially exposed to fetal blood. It plays no role in the prevention of erythroblastosis fetalis because of anti-Kell antibodies. Educational Objective: Antigens on the fetal RBCs depend on the antigens of each parent's RBCs. If the mother exhibits antibodies against a specific RBC antigen, whether from a previous pregnancy or a blood transfusion, the fetus is at risk for erythroblastosis fetalis if it carries that antigen, as maternal lgG antibodies can cross the placenta. The first step in determining the potential RBC antigens of a fetus is to determine the antigen type of each parent. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An otherwise healthy 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period . She is 150 cm (4 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m 2• Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. The cervix is visualized , and the vaginal mucosa is hypoestrogenized . Serum studies show a luteinizing hormone concentration of 22 mlU/mL , follicle-stimulating hormone concentration of 33 mlU/mL , and prolactin concentration of 9 ng/ml. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Turner syndrome is a common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is secondary to gonadal (ovarian) dysgenesis in the setting of a 45,XO genotype. Other signs of Turner syndrome include a short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. Additionally, as a result of decreased estrogen concentrations, patients fail to develop mature secondary sexual characteristics of breast and pubic hair development. As well, patients may develop vaginal atrophy or dryness related to low estrogen concentrations, like postmenopausal patients. Vital signs will be within normal limits, and diagnosis is made through a karyotype analysis. Other labs that may aid in diagnosis are increased concentrations of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle­ stimulating hormone (FSH) as a result of the lack of negative feedback from estrogen, but these findings are nonspecific.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Anorexia nervosa (Choice A) presents with extremely low body weight, fear of weight gain, and dysphoria, as well as bradycardia and lanugo on physical examination. While it can present with amenorrhea as a result of suppression of the hypothalamic-ovarian-pituitary axis, it is unlikely in this patient with an overweight BMI. Congenital absence of the uterus (Choice B) is because of an error in the normal development of the Mullerian system that results in complete absence of the uterus and, occasionally, the upper vagina. However, these patients will have functional ovaries and therefore adequate maturation of secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast and pubic hair development. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice D) presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, most commonly to the result of a pituitary gland adenoma. High concentrations of prolactin inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone and subsequently cause decreased concentrations of FSH and LH. This patient's prolactin concentration is within reference ranges. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Choice E) leads to amenorrhea as caused by the decreased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, FSH, and LH, which results in impaired follicle maturation and ovulation, as well as a lack of development of secondary sexual characteristics. This patient's FSH and LH are within reference ranges, making this an unlikely diagnosis. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (Choice F) most commonly presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and irregular menses because of anovulation secondary to increased androgen concentrations. The LH to FSH ratio is typically increased, and ultrasonography of the pelvis will show numerous ovarian follicular cysts. It is more commonly associated with secondary oligomenorrhea than primary amenorrhea. Pregnancy (Choice G) causes amenorrhea as the endometrial lining is maintained to support the developing embryo. However, it typically causes secondary amenorrhea in a sexually active patient, rather than primary amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea, which is because of ovarian dysgenesis. Other signs include the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, short stature, cystic hygroma or webbed neck, swelling in the hands and feet, coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, fused kidney, and infertility. LH and FSH concentrations are typically increased because of the absence of negative feedback from estrogen, and diagnosis is made with a karyotype analysis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of heavy vaginal bleeding for the past 3 days. She has no history of serious illness. Menopause occurred 6 years ago. A Pap smear 1 year ago showed no abnormalities . Physical examination today shows no abnormalities . Pelvic examination shows an irregularly shaped uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation . Her hemoglobin concentration is 9 g/dl , and hematocrit is 27%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration
choices.C: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Abnormal uterine bleeding should be suspected when bleeding is irregular, unpredictable, or not associated with usual premenstrual signs and symptoms (eg, bloating, breast fullness, uterine cramps). It may be caused by structural abnormalities such as cervical or endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, endometrial hyperplasia, malignancy, inflammation or infection of the genital tract, coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endocrine dysfunction (eg, thyroid disorders, prolactin, androgens), iatrogenic, or idiopathic. In postmenopausal patients and patients over the age of 45, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The most appropriate next step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. If a patient cannot tolerate an outpatient procedure or if the outpatient sampling is nondiagnostic, a dilation and curettage or hysteroscopy can be performed. A hysteroscopy with sampling allows for a more complete evaluation of the endometrium (eg, polyps, myomas, structural abnormalities).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentration (Choice A) would not disclose the cause of abnormal uterine bleeding in this patient. FSH is increased in postmenopausal patients but is not useful in the evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding. In endometrial carcinoma, the measurement of cancer antigen 125 can be used for the surveillance of patients' disease progression. MRI of the pelvis (Choice B) may be used to evaluate myometrial, cervical, or lymph node invasion and metastasis of endometrial carcinoma but is infrequently used. MRI would not be the next step in the evaluation for endometrial carcinoma, which is more definitively evaluated by tissue sampling. Transfusion of packed red blood cells (Choice C) is generally not necessary in a stable patient with a hemoglobin concentration greater than 7 g/dl. The patient in the question has a hemoglobin of 9 g/dl and does not meet criteria to receive a transfusion at this time. Hysterectomy (Choice E) may be indicated if endometrial carcinoma is diagnosed. However, in a patient with abnormal uterine bleeding, prior steps need to be taken to diagnose the cause of the abnormal uterine bleeding. Educational Objective: Abnormal uterine bleeding refers to irregular menstrual bleeding that may be abnormal in quality, duration, or timing. In postmenopausal patients and patients over the age of 45, there is a higher risk for endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy. The next appropriate step in evaluation would be an endometrial biopsy to evaluate for the presence of endometrial cancer. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of nausea, urinary frequency , and fatigue for 2 months . She has never had a menstrual period. Breast development is Tanner stage 4. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m 2• Physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.C: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone concentrations

correctExplanation: Clinicians should maintain a low threshold of suspicion for pregnancy in adolescent and teenage patients who are at high risk for unintended pregnancy. Pregnancy should always be considered as a potential cause of presumed primary amenorrhea and should be excluded before considering other causes. Early symptoms of pregnancy include fatigue, nausea, urinary frequency, and irregular menstruation. A careful history should be taken, including of the patient's menstrual history, sexual activity, contraceptive usage, and the possibility of pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test should be obtained if it is possible that the patient may be pregnant.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Complete blood count (Choice A) is useful in the diagnosis of anemia, which may be caused by iron deficiency in menstruating females. Anemia also presents with symptoms of lightheadedness, diaphoresis, and pallor. Measurement of serum estrogen concentration (Choice B) may reflect abnormalities in the ovarian production of estrogen and may disclose the cause of primary amenorrhea, such as gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome). This patient presents with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics, suggesting normal estrogen concentrations. Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone concentrations (Choice C) may disclose hypothalamic or pituitary disorders that lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and primary amenorrhea. Patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism will usually not present with Tanner stage 4 secondary sexual characteristics. A progesterone challenge test (Choice E) is useful for distinguishing outflow tract disorders from hormonal etiologies of amenorrhea. Educational Objective: Pregnancy should always be considered as a potential etiology of presumed primary amenorrhea and should be excluded before considering other causes. Early symptoms of pregnancy include fatigue, nausea, urinary frequency, and irregular menstruation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A healthy 22-year-old primigravid woman at 33 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of heavy, painless vaginal bleeding for 30 minutes . Pregnancy had been uncomplicated . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Examination shows a nontender uterus consistent in size with a 33-week gestation . The vertex is not engaged in the pelvis . Speculum examination shows vaginal bleeding from a closed cervix . The fetal heart rate is 140/min. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
correctExplanation: Causes of vaginal bleeding in the third trimester include, but are not limited to, trauma to the vagina or cervix from intercourse, cervical ectropion, cervicitis, uterine rupture, placental abruption, placenta accreta, increta, or percreta, vasa previa, and placenta previa. Placenta previa is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or completely overlies the internal cervical os. Placenta previa is usually detected on routine prenatal ultrasonography. Its most common presenting symptom is painless vaginal bleeding during the third trimester. The incidence of placenta previa is higher earlier in pregnancy and decreases with increasing gestational age as the placenta often migrates cephalad. If mild, bleeding from placenta previa may self-terminate within several hours. However, severe bleeding from placenta previa may lead to hemorrhagic shock, which is associated with maternal tachycardia, hypotension, decreased organ perfusion, and eventual organ failure. Fetal distress will generally also be present. Treatment of hemorrhagic shock from placenta previa involves cesarean delivery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amniotic fluid embolism (Choice A) is a rare complication of childbirth and occurs during delivery or immediately postpartum as a result of amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation. It presents with shortness of breath, altered mental status, hypoxia, and hypotension. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, cardiovascular collapse, and maternal and/or fetal death. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice B) can be a complication of amniotic fluid embolism and occurs because of a pathologic activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to microthrombi, consumption of platelets, and coagulopathy that is characterized by both thrombosis and hemorrhage. Sepsis (Choice D) occurs from severe infections and is characterized by an inflammatory and organ-dysfunctional state. Pregnant patients are susceptible to several types of infections, including urinary tract infections which may present with fever and dysuria, and chorioamnionitis which typically presents with fever, tachycardia, and uterine tenderness. Uterine rupture (Choice E) is a dangerous complication of pregnancy wherein the muscular wall of the uterus tears. Severe pain is a common initial finding. Hemodynamic instability can manifest in the mother with tachycardia and hypotension, and in the fetus with late decelerations, tachycardia, bradycardia, or loss of beat-to-beat variability. Risk factors for uterine rupture include vaginal birth after cesarean delivery, multiparity, and induction of labor with prostaglandin analogues or oxytocin. Educational Objective: Placenta previa is an abnormal positioning of placental tissue such that the placenta partially or entirely overlies the internal cervical os. It can spontaneously resolve, but if it persists into the third trimester, may result in painless vaginal bleeding. Severe bleeding from placenta previa may lead to hemorrhagic shock, and treatment involves cesarean delivery. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the physician with her partner because she has been unable to conceive for 18 months . She also has had moderate dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals and last 5 days. Examination of the patient and her partner, including physical examination , semen analysis , testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae , serial urinalyses to document luteinizing hormone surge , in-phase endometrial biopsy, and hysterosalpingography , shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is most likely associated with this patient's infertility?
correctExplanation: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus, and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Local inflammatory responses to ectopic endometrial cells cause abdominal and pelvic pain, which may be severe. The pain is often cyclic in response to fluctuating hormone concentrations during the menstrual cycle. The standard for diagnosis is a diagnostic laparoscopy, which evaluates for visual evidence of ectopic endometriotic implant lesions and permits obtaining samples for histology. Chronic inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes leads to infertility in many women with endometriosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hyperprolactinemia (Choice B) causes growth of glandular breast tissue and presents with unexpected lactation (galactorrhea). Inappropriate elevation of prolactin often arises from a hyperfunctioning anterior pituitary microadenoma. Dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia are not typical symptoms of hyperprolactinemia. Hypothyroidism (Choice C) presents with weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. It may also result in amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea. Inadequate cervical mucus (Choice D) is a cause of infertility but is not associated with symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia, which are more suggestive of endometriosis. Pelvic adhesions (Choice E) are a delayed result of surgery, infection (eg, pelvic inflammatory disease), or chronic inflammation from severe endometriosis. While pelvic adhesions may be present and cause abdominal pain in some patients with endometriosis, infertility in most cases is directly related to ectopic endometrial tissue and associated inflammation and scarring within the fallopian tubes, rather than pelvic adhesions. Educational Objective: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside of the uterus, and classically presents with symptoms of abdominal and pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia. Many patients experience infertility as a result of inflammation and scarring of the fallopian tubes. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 69-year-old nulliparous white woman has the sudden onset of severe pain in the upper back after sitting down. She has hypertension treated with a ~-adrenergic blocking agent. She drinks one alcoholic beverage with dinner each night. An x-ray of the spine shows a compression fracture of the 10th thoracic vertebra . Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for this condition?
correctExplanation: Osteoporosis is a common condition that is characterized by the progressive loss of bone mineral density leading to decreased bone strength. This decreased bone mineral density often leads to fragility fractures, such as in this patient, who experienced a thoracic compression fracture with a minimal axial load when sitting. Osteoporosis and resultant fractures can greatly decrease mobility, even leading to death in elderly individuals. The disease classically affects postmenopausal women with inflammatory disorders, and individuals with metabolic or endocrine disorders, such as hypercortisolism or hyperparathyroidism. Osteoporosis can be induced by long-term treatment with medications that cause an increase in bone resorption, such as corticosteroids. Osteoporosis tends to affect females at a higher rate than males, especially those of Caucasian ethnicity. Males generally develop higher peak bone mass during the first 30 years of life. Given the chronic and generally linear rate of bone mineral loss, males will therefore retain higher bone mineral density for a longer period given the higher bone mineral density starting point than females. As testosterone and estrogen both stimulate osteoblasts and increase or maintain bone mineral density, the loss of estrogen leads to an accelerated loss of bone mass in post-menopausal women.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol use (Choice A) has a negative effect on bone mineral density; however, this effect is mostly seen with heavy drinking over many years. Alcohol is a diuretic and can cause loss of electrolytes, including calcium. Hypertension (Choice B) is associated with low bone mineral density; however, it is not as significant of a risk factor as genetic predisposition by race. The use of antihypertensive medications may also be a protective factor. Nulliparity (Choice C) may be associated with low bone mineral density but to a lesser extent than conditions that shorten or reduce the amount or duration of estrogen stimulus on bone, such as early menopause, smoking, low BMI, and late menarche. Use of a ~-adrenergic blocking agent (Choice E) is not generally a significant risk factor for the development of osteoporosis. The use of ~-adrenergic blockers has been associated with increased bone mineral density and decreased fracture risk. Educational Objective: Osteoporosis is a progressive loss of bone mineral density that occurs with aging and can lead to fragility fractures. Risk factors include female gender, Caucasian ethnicity, chronic inflammatory disease, use of corticosteroids, adrenal, thyroid, or parathyroid disease, sedentary lifestyle, and low estrogen states. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous
